sections.title: Cap and form
sections.text: Leccinum scabrum, the brown birch bolete, produces a medium to large fruitbody. Its cap is usually 4–20 cm wide, convex at first and later expanding; colour ranges from grey-brown or yellow-brown to darker brown, sometimes becoming olive-tinged with age. The surface is smooth to slightly velvety, dry or somewhat viscid in wet weather, and may crack as it ages.

sections.title: Tubes, pores and stem
sections.text: The cap underside bears whitish tubes that darken to greyish or brownish as they mature, not gills. Their openings are small, round pores, cream to grey-beige, sometimes staining slightly yellowish when handled. The pale stem is slender to club-shaped, often long relative to the cap, and dotted with small grey-brown to blackish scales (scabers) that darken with age. It has no ring or volva.

sections.title: Flesh and habitat
sections.text: Flesh is white and firm in young specimens; it changes little when cut, although it may sometimes become faintly brownish or slowly pinkish, and localized colour changes are reported near the stem base. Taste and smell are mild or indistinct. This is an ectomycorrhizal fungus associated with birches (Betula), growing on the ground in open woods, heaths and damp sites, mainly in summer and autumn. The spore deposit is olive-brown.

sections.title: Identification and food safety
sections.text: The brown cap, pale stem with dark scabers, and growth beneath birch are useful characters, but closely related rough-stemmed boletes can be difficult to distinguish. The DGfM positive list includes L. scabrum s.l. among edible mushrooms; this does not replace reliable identification. Eat it only thoroughly cooked, never raw or undercooked. A 2014 NAMA report of illness after raw consumption concerned a specimen reported as L. alaskanum or L. scabrum; that determination does not establish L. scabrum as the cause. Do not eat a mushroom based only on this page or its image.

traits: Convex then expanding cap, 4–20 cm, grey-brown to yellow-brown or darker; dry to slightly viscid in wet weather
Whitish tubes darkening greyish to brownish with age, ending in small round pores — never gills
Pale, slender stem dotted with grey-brown to blackish scabers; no ring or volva
White flesh, usually changing little when cut but sometimes staining faintly brownish or pinkish
Ectomycorrhizal with birches, growing on the ground, mainly in summer and autumn; olive-brown spore print
safetyNote: The DGfM positive list includes Leccinum scabrum s.l. among edible mushrooms; this does not replace reliable identification. Eat it only thoroughly cooked, never raw or undercooked. A photograph or this page alone is not enough to decide that a mushroom is safe to eat. Contact a poison centre or emergency services if symptoms develop after ingestion.
